title: Delivery Emergencies — Shoulder Dystocia, Cord Prolapse, Abruption
sources: Critical Vector — OB Pocket Guide: Shoulder Dystocia / Cord Prolapse / Placental Abruption (ACOG 2023)

changelog.change: Initial entry — the HELPERR sequence for shoulder dystocia, the cord-prolapse steps, and placental abruption recognition + management.

summary: Shoulder dystocia: call for help, McRoberts + suprapubic (NOT fundal) pressure first, then internal rotation / deliver the posterior arm / all-fours. Cord prolapse: elevate the presenting part continuously and go to an emergent caesarean — do not replace the cord. Abruption: painful bleeding + a rigid tender uterus + fetal distress ± DIC.

body.text: Time-critical — aim to deliver within ~5 minutes of recognition (rising risk of hypoxic injury and brachial plexus injury). Note the time. Do NOT apply fundal pressure and do NOT apply excessive downward traction on the head.

items: H — Help: call additional OB, NICU / paediatrics, and anaesthesia NOW.
E — Evaluate for episiotomy: only if needed for room to perform internal manoeuvres (it does not relieve a bony impaction).
L — Legs: McRoberts — hyperflex the maternal thighs onto the abdomen (flattens the lumbar lordosis, rotates the symphysis). Resolves ~40% alone.
P — suprapubic Pressure: continuous or rocking, directed downward and laterally onto the fetal anterior shoulder — NOT fundal pressure.

E — Enter (internal rotation): Rubin II (pressure on the posterior aspect of the anterior shoulder → adduction), then add Woods screw (rotate the posterior shoulder anteriorly) or reverse Woods screw.
R — Remove the posterior arm: sweep it across the fetal chest and deliver the hand / forearm (highly effective).
R — Roll: the Gaskin all-fours manoeuvre (mother onto hands and knees), then reattempt delivery of the posterior (now uppermost) shoulder.
Last resort: deliberate clavicle fracture; Zavanelli manoeuvre (cephalic replacement → caesarean); symphysiotomy.

body.text: The moment it's recognised (palpable pulsating cord, or a fetal bradycardia after membrane rupture), the decision-to-delivery clock is running.

items: 1. Call for help; activate the obstetric emergency / OR.
2. Manually elevate the presenting part off the cord with a gloved hand, and KEEP it there continuously (into the OR).
4. Fill the bladder with 500–750 mL of saline (if time allows) to elevate the presenting part and reduce cord compression.
5. Emergent caesarean delivery (a rapid instrumental vaginal delivery only if the cervix is fully dilated and the head is low).

Do NOT try to replace the cord into the uterus. Keep an exposed cord warm and moist with saline-soaked gauze; handle it minimally (spasm). Stop oxytocin; a tocolytic (terbutaline) can be given as a bridge.

Painful vaginal bleeding (in ~80%; 10–20% is concealed — the bleeding is retroplacental and the visible loss underestimates it). A 'woody', rigid, tender uterus with high-frequency low-amplitude contractions. Fetal heart-rate abnormalities. DIC in severe cases (abruption is the commonest obstetric cause).
Risk factors: hypertension / preeclampsia, abdominal trauma, cocaine, smoking, prior abruption, PPROM, polyhydramnios with rapid decompression.
Minor and stable, remote from term: continuous monitoring, antenatal corticosteroids if < 34 weeks, anti-D if Rh-negative — deliver for maternal or fetal instability.

Major abruption: immediate delivery (caesarean unless delivery is imminent), activate the MTP, replace fibrinogen aggressively (target > 150–200 mg/dL — cryoprecipitate / concentrate), and correct the DIC. Expect a Couvelaire uterus and atony — have uterotonics ready.
Rh-negative: send a Kleihauer-Betke and dose anti-D (RhoGAM) accordingly.

buildNote: Tier 1. Uterine inversion and uterine rupture are further intrapartum emergencies to add. Vacuum / forceps criteria are separate.
